accepted_deviations.summary: Profile-relay assignment hashes the pubkey, so two contacts can land on the same pool relay; collisions follow the birthday bound (~79% for a 5-member roster over the 8-relay pool). Collision-free-per-roster assignment would require the profile module to know roster membership, which its import boundary forbids by design.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not claim 'no relay ever learns two members of the same circle', nor 'no single server sees everyone you look up'. The spreading claim must stay statistical and must keep the collision sentence beside it.

accepted_deviations.summary: A peer's assignment salt is private to their install, so Haven cannot know which pool relay a peer reads from; publishing the user's own kind-0 therefore targets the ENTIRE usable pool. Every pool relay learns (our pubkey, our IP), and one that also serves our reads can link identity to our ~1/N contact sample.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not claim profile publishing is limited to a subset of the pool, nor that profile publishing is unlinkable to the identity. It MAY state that reads are unauthenticated (the fetch path is built with no signer and structurally cannot answer NIP-42).

accepted_deviations.summary: Haven publishes no NIP-65 / kind-10002 relay list naming the profile pool, because that event is identity-signed and publicly fetchable and would rebuild the cross-plane link the pool exists to break. Accepted cost: outbox-model external clients may fail to resolve a Haven profile. Enforced by check_profile_privacy_boundaries.sh Check 10 and by RelayType::Profile::to_kind() returning None.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not imply that no relay can ever learn a device uses it for the profile plane — a pool relay sees that traffic directly. Only the narrower claim is true: Haven never publishes a list naming the profile relays, so a relay OUTSIDE the pool has no public pointer to it.

accepted_deviations.summary: The kind-0 merge base is fetched from the profile pool only — a deliberate reversal of the MEDIUM-4 fix (self_merge_base_relays deleted). A Haven save can therefore drop kind-0 fields another client set on relays outside the pool.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not claim that editing your profile in Haven preserves everything set by another Nostr client. NOTE: no user-facing string discloses this today — see the report's disclosure-gap section; no invariant references P4 because filing one would require inventing a disclosure that does not exist.

accepted_deviations.summary: The per-install profile-relay assignment salt is NEVER rotated: rotation discloses each contact to an additional relay, converging on full disclosure, so a stable salt is strictly better in aggregate. Accepted cost: the assigned relay accumulates a durable 'this IP is persistently interested in this pubkey' observation. Bounded by PROFILE_MAX_RELAY_RANK = 2 and destroyed by two distinct paths (wipe_all_profiles; deletion of the circles.db file set).
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not present the stable pairing as a pure benefit, and must not claim the pairing 'never changes' — the retry ladder reaches a second relay and rendezvous ranking shifts when the pool changes. State the bound as at most TWO of the eight, and keep the durable-record cost sentence alongside the spreading claim.

accepted_deviations.summary: Haven ships no Tor or proxy support. A pool relay, a circle relay, the tile provider and any host serving a co-member's profile picture all observe the user's real IP on publish and on read. The salted partition limits WHAT a relay learns, not WHO it is talking to.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must make no network-level unlinkability or anonymity claim, and must never say Haven hides your IP address. A VPN may be described as the mitigation, attributed to the VPN, never to Haven.

accepted_deviations.summary: The contamination ledger is append-only because contamination is historical — a relay that routed a circle's kind-445 last month saw those events, and leaving does not un-see them. Welcome-delivery relays were persisted nowhere before the change, so refresh_contamination_ledger cannot fold them in and will not exclude them.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not claim that leaving a circle removes all relay exposure, nor that the contamination warnings cover every relay that has ever carried this identity's traffic.

accepted_deviations.summary: Post-join leaf-key self-update — a SHOULD in protocol-core/joining.md, carried forward from the retired MIP-02 which stated it as a MUST within 24 h — is disabled (enablePeriodicSelfUpdate = false). The MIP-03 successor protocol-core/group-messaging.md states no periodic-rotation requirement at all, so the earlier 'MIP-03 SHOULD' framing overstated the deviation. Keys rotate only on membership change.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must never say keys rotate regularly or periodically, and must never use this locale's term for forward secrecy. Key change may only be described as following membership change. The spec's own words support this: 'a member who never rotates is a forward-secrecy weakness for itself' (protocol-core/joining.md).

accepted_deviations.summary: NOT one connection per relay: Haven opens at least TWO long-lived nostr-sdk Clients per process — the live-sync engine's receive client (build_engine_client, haven-core/src/relay/live_sync/session.rs:92) and the publish client (RelayManager::new, haven-core/src/relay/manager.rs:412) — plus one more for every isolate that builds its own RelayManager, which the Android background-sharing foreground service does. A shared relay therefore sees two or three connections from the same address, not one, and can join them by source address without any protocol help. A relay serving BOTH the gift-wrap inbox (kind 1059 by #p = user pubkey) and group messages (kind 445 by #h = nostr_group_id) over the same connection can correlate the real identity pubkey with circle membership by connection continuity. Since M11 the receive connection is STANDING while the app is FOREGROUNDED, on both platforms, so the correlation is continuous rather than bursty for as long as that socket is held. Since P4 it is no longer standing while backgrounded on iOS either: with background sharing on the engine is PAUSED between publishes and both filters ride one bounded burst per publish tick, so for a CIRCLE relay the join is per-burst rather than continuous. Per-burst is NOT per-publish, though since PUB-COALESCE it is close to it: a burst re-anchors every circle's #h REQ, connects the whole relay union AND publishes every publish-eligible circle, so a circle relay sees a REQ/CLOSE pair on every burst and this device's kind-445 for its own circle on essentially every burst too. The join stays wider than the send in three cases only — a burst whose publish window refuses publishes nothing at all; a subscribed circle that is not publish-eligible (isLegacyOrphaned, or engine-flagged Unrecoverable) is re-anchored on every burst and never published to; a send that fails, is deferred by the engine, or is the tail of a roster past kMaxCirclesPerBurst. What coalescing ADDS to this deviation is a duration: the union connection is held across the whole staggered publish pass, so its connect-to-disconnect span grows with the number of eligible circles and hands EVERY relay in the union — one carrying a single circle, or an inbox relay carrying none — an estimator of that count, which the per-circle schedules leaked only as a rate and only to relays that already read the circle set off the multiplexed #h filter (PUB-COALESCE). That NARROWS the deviation for circle relays without strictly narrowing it: an inbox-ONLY relay (kind-10050 inbox, none of this account's circles — an independent set) carries no kind-445 to correlate with, and where it used to see one continuous socket it now sees a REQ/CLOSE pair every 72-168 s (the 120 s nominal cadence, jittered ±40 %), which is itself the inference "this pubkey is background-sharing right now". The lever is INBOX_BURSTS_PER_REQ (OD4-b, accepted, blocked on a separate defect and not yet raised); at the shipped value that inference is a named, disclosed residual, not a mitigated one. The residuals P4 carries are enumerated in SECURITY.md under "iOS background sharing: presence only at publish instants (P4)". On Android it no longer outlives the foreground: since P1 the pause path stops the engine in BOTH toggle states (with sharing ON it stops first to hand the MLS session to the foreground service; with sharing OFF `_stopLiveSyncBounded()` stops it and deliberately does not release the guard, since no isolate reclaims it), and the resume heal restarts it. Not protocol-forced: the kind-10050 inbox list and the group's 0x8004 relay set are independent, and seeding them disjointly — as the profile pool already is — would remove the single-socket join. Declined because it doubles connection count and because P6 (no Tor/proxy) leaves IP-level joining intact; recorded so the trade-off stays re-decidable.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not claim relays cannot link your identity to your circle membership, and must not present the ephemeral per-message kind-445 author keys as making you unlinkable at the relay.

accepted_deviations.summary: Per-circle publish schedules are replaced by ONE coalesced burst per jittered interval that publishes every publish-eligible circle, so radio wakes fall from about N x 30/h to about 30/h. Shared-relay decorrelation was never effective while the multiplexed #h subscription and the single publish socket exist — a shared relay reads the circle set straight off the filter — so what is given up is only weak protection against colluding relays that ignore IP. THREE costs are accepted. (1) RECORDED: with one shared tick sequence, circles held on DISJOINT relay sets emit identical inter-burst intervals, so anyone holding two of your circles' relay archives — each relay carrying only ONE of those circles — can tell the two circles belong to the same phone. (2) The circle COUNT becomes a single-relay observable, and WHICH SOCKET carries it splits by plane. The burst holds its connection across the whole staggered publish pass, so the span grows with the number of eligible circles. Backgrounded on iOS that connection is the engine socket over the entire relay union (every circle's relays and the inbox relays), measurable server-side by any relay in that union — one carrying only one of your circles, and an inbox-only relay carrying none. On the ANDROID FOREGROUND SERVICE there is no engine socket at all, so the publish pool IS the carrier: RelayManager::shutdown is a COLLECTIVE client.disconnect(), and the service calls it at step 9b of every delivery cycle and again in onDestroy, so a relay carrying exactly one circle in a pass sees connect-at-its-own-publish through disconnect-at-teardown — a tail that grows with the circles published AFTER it and, over the CSPRNG burst permutation, converges to the whole pass length. In the FOREGROUND there is no collective disconnect: publish_relay_options() is ping(false).reconnect(false).sleep_when_idle(true).idle_timeout(10 s), polled once a minute from inside the connection task, so each relay's socket sleeps independently in (60 s, 70 s] after that relay's own last send and measures only its own span. The old scheme leaked N only as a RATE, and only to shared relays that already read it off the multiplexed filter; the new one leaks it as a DURATION, to relays that previously could not know it at all. kMaxCirclesPerAccount (10) bounds the roster and therefore the estimator, one circle under the kMaxCirclesPerBurst (11) at which the per-gap ceiling saturates. (3) N ALSO LEAKS THROUGH THE SIGNED TIMESTAMPS, and that carrier persists. PublishStagger.maxGapFor is deterministic and INJECTIVE over n = 5..10, the whole range kMaxCirclesPerAccount admits (only 2, 3 and 4 collapse, all three at the 9 s ceiling), and the expected whole-burst span rises monotonically with it: about 5.5 s at two circles, 11 at three, 16.5 at four, up to 24 s at ten. An observer holding kind-445 archives of two of your circles — exactly the adversary cost (1) hands the LINK to — reads one whole-second delta per burst; over a handful of bursts the largest delta estimates the burst span (monotone in n) and the lowest cluster's upper edge estimates the per-gap ceiling. That ceiling does NOT invert to a single n: created_at is whole seconds and the millisecond injectivity does not survive the quantization, so the observable alphabet resolves the roster exactly at five and six circles, to a PAIR at seven/eight and nine/ten (which share {2..5} and {2,3,4}), and to the TRIPLE two/three/four below that (which share {2..9}). Separating a pair needs the span term or the delta FREQUENCIES rather than the ceiling, i.e. more bursts - a cost in samples and not a bound, so the count still leaks, one bit coarser on those two pairs. A relay carrying several of your circles reads adjacent pairs directly and converges faster. It is worse than cost (2)'s duration in three ways: it needs no socket observation at all (a passive archive scraper suffices), connection noise does not defeat it, and it PERSISTS, because the delta is inside the SIGNED event and therefore in every archive of it. It compounds with cost (1) — link, then count. kMaxCirclesPerAccount bounds the estimate at ten, which is a ceiling on the estimate and not a mitigation. The CSPRNG stagger is retained with its constants unmoved, and its claim is NARROWED TWICE. It is not 'the archive-adversary defence', because after coalescing the archive reader gets the link anyway from the shared inter-burst interval sequence. And what it buys is ROSTER-SCOPED rather than a flat eight values: maxGapFor prices every gap at the burst's OWN size, so the observable whole-second delta alphabet thins monotonically — {2..9} (eight values) up to four circles, {2..6} at six, {2..5} at eight, and {2,3,4} at kMaxCirclesPerAccount (10), the largest burst a bounded roster can produce; maxGapFor keeps answering one circle further, where the alphabet is {2,3}, and no observer reaches that while the bound holds. Coalescing caused the thinning: pre-P5 every gap was priced at the default totalPublishes = 2, so the alphabet was always eight — and the eight-value proof cited on INV-R-PER-CIRCLE-PUBLISH-DECORRELATED draws at that same default, so it pins only the n = 2 case. At small rosters the downgrade in KIND is real: a byte-identical created_at is a zero-cost equality join over a whole-network index (created_at_A == created_at_B, decisive on one burst), while eight admissible offsets force a windowed correlation that needs a targeted hypothesis about which two circles share a device. AT THE ROSTER BOUND IT BARELY IS: a three-element alphabet is three shifted equality joins over that same whole-network index, still un-targeted mass linkage, so what survives at ten circles is a constant factor rather than a change in kind. Owner decision OD3, accepted 2026-08-29; the eleven-circle burst cap and its own residual are owner decision 2026-09-08 option (a), and the TEN-circle account roster bound that puts the cap's deferral branch out of production reach is owner decision 2026-09-09 — both recorded on INV-W-445-EXPIRATION-WINDOW.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not present per-circle timing as preventing a relay from linking your circles, must not limit that linkage to relays that carry SEVERAL of your circles (a relay holding one of them, plus an archive of another, is enough), and must not present the stagger as buying more than the NUMBER of distinct whole-second timestamps it produces — a number that is roster-dependent and falls to three at kMaxCirclesPerAccount — and in particular not as 'the archive-adversary defence', which it stopped being when the schedules were coalesced. Copy must equally not claim that a relay learns nothing about how many circles you are in, and must not scope that leak to a single carrier. There are three: the burst's connect-to-disconnect span at any relay that sees a burst (an inbox-only relay included); the same span on the PUBLISH POOL wherever that pool is COLLECTIVELY disconnected at teardown (the iOS-background burst and the Android foreground service); and the SIGNED kind-445 created_at deltas themselves, whose per-gap ceiling resolves the circle count exactly at five and six circles and to a PAIR or a TRIPLE otherwise - one bit coarser on those, never absent - and which persist in any archive of the events.

accepted_deviations.summary: Owner-directed reversal (recorded 2026-07-12, made public-by-default 2026-07-16) of Security Rule 10's no-public-profiles posture: the kind-0 + Blossom public profile module deliberately publishes the display name and photo, unconditionally, on save. Onboarding pre-fills an anonymous pseudonym and publishes it; there is no skip / pubkey-only path and no consent toggle. Its remaining boundaries are CI-enforced by check_profile_privacy_boundaries.sh.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not say a saved name or photo 'may be' published, must not imply a setting exists that keeps them private, and must not offer a circles-only name. Equally, this must not be described as a regression to be reverted.

accepted_deviations.summary: On iOS the SQLCipher DB keys use kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly rather than the library default kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlocked, so a background wake can open the database while the device is locked. Owner-approved to enable locked-device background location sharing.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not claim a locked phone protects Haven's data at rest. A still-powered-on device unlocked at least once since boot can have the OS surrender the DB key WHILE LOCKED; only a device powered off and not yet unlocked keeps it sealed. NOTE: no user-facing string discloses this today — see docs/privacy/README.md, known gaps.

accepted_deviations.summary: Owner decision D8 (2026-08-28) accepts the iOS backup posture UNCHANGED now that circles.db carries the member directory — the payload change D5 said would deserve its own decision on its own timeline. The Haven data directory is getApplicationDocumentsDirectory() + '/haven' with no platform branch (haven/lib/src/services/data_directory_provider.dart:44-47), so on iOS circles.db, its -journal sidecar and session.sqlite sit in Documents/, the most-backed-up location the OS offers, and NSURLIsExcludedFromBackupKey appears NOWHERE in the tree — not in haven/ios/Runner/, not in any Dart or Rust path, not in a checked-in plugin. Android is unaffected: allowBackup="false" with no dataExtractionRules and no fullBackupContent (haven/android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:48), so the posture is asymmetric and one-sided. What travels into a backup is ciphertext whose key is a ThisDeviceOnly Keychain item (see IOS-KEYCHAIN), so a restore onto a DIFFERENT device cannot open it; a SAME-DEVICE restore can, and reinstates a snapshot taken before a logout or a Delete Identity. wipe_all_mls_state deletes circles.db and session.sqlite with their sidecars and destroys both keyring entries (haven/rust_builder/src/api.rs:877, :983-986), but that destruction is DEVICE-LOCAL rather than absolute and no code Haven can write reaches into a backup to finish it.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not claim that logging out or deleting your identity IRREVERSIBLY destroys the on-device member directory — nor anything else living in circles.db — because a same-device restore from an iOS backup can bring the encrypted file back. The claim that IS true is bounded: the deletion removes the file set from this device, and what a backup carries cannot be opened on a different device. Copy must equally not present the backup as harmless because it is encrypted — 'another device cannot read it' is the true half; 'a backup holds nothing of yours' is not. NOTE: no user-facing string discloses this today. identityAdvancedDeleteBody stays inside the line by describing the act ('deletes your identity and all circle data from this phone') and asserting no permanence; the member-directory disclosure (owner decision D6) has had no surface since the Settings → Privacy page was removed on 2026-08-29, and no invariant carries status accepted_deviation against this entry yet; since that date a zero-disclosure accepted deviation is a permitted state (docs/privacy/README.md), so filing one is a deliberate act rather than an impossibility — the same holds for P4. INV-D-DIRECTORY-NEVER-LEAVES-SQLCIPHER stays 'enforced' and names this deviation in its statement and its note.

accepted_deviations.summary: The engine's stored convergence buffer has no per-group cap and no eviction API (upstream MDK #757, OPEN). A Haven-side intake cap throttles ingest but cannot bound engine storage — an accepted insider-threat storage-DoS exposure.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not claim a circle member cannot consume unbounded device storage. Security Rule 12's backpressure bounds the FETCH, not the engine's buffer.

accepted_deviations.summary: kind-445 application messages carry a DETERMINISTIC NIP-40 expiration. The retired per-send design sampled it precisely to avoid a constant-TTL fingerprint identifying Haven clients among mixed MLS-over-Nostr traffic; group-level retention is what the protocol now offers, so the fingerprint is accepted. The send-side bound (RetentionBoundPeeler) BROADENED it, and that widening is accepted here too: the delta is no longer fixed at group creation, it is decided at SEND time, and Haven now stamps 228 s in circles it did not create — where it previously stamped nothing. So the discriminator is no longer only client-wide. In a circle whose declared message-retention.v1 window is absent, zero, or longer than 228 s, `expiration - created_at == 228` separates the Haven member's location updates from every other member's traffic on the same #h: a PER-MEMBER discriminator inside one group, sharper than the client-wide one because it attributes traffic within a group whose membership a relay cannot otherwise resolve. Accepted as the price of the two properties the bound buys — bounded relay residency, and location traffic not masquerading as membership traffic. A circle Haven created is unaffected: there every member stamps the same 228 s.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not present the expiry as making Haven traffic less distinguishable. It does the opposite, in two ways: the constant is a client-wide discriminator visible to any relay or member, and inside a circle whose declared window is absent, zero, or longer than 228 s it is additionally a per-member one, because Haven's 228 s then differs from what that circle's other clients stamp (or from their stamping nothing); a circle declaring SHORTER is the one foreign case with no per-member split, since Haven stamps that declared value like every other client. Copy must also not imply the expiry follows the circle's own policy — Haven applies its own window whether or not the circle asked for one — and the value cannot be changed for circles that already exist.

accepted_deviations.summary: The corroboration gate deliberately keeps NO admin-side record of a departing member's intent, so there is no automatic admin-side backstop. In the conjunction of: the leaver crashes mid-leave, AND its SelfRemove was deferred or lost the order race, AND it never re-opens the app — no removal commit is ever produced and a stale roster ghost stays authorized until an admin manually removes it. SECURITY.md labels this 'Precisely-bounded residual (accepted)'.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not state that leaving always re-keys the circle within a bounded time. The automatically-unconverged case needs a manual admin removal and there is no admin-visible signal one is owed. NOTE: no user-facing string discloses this. The Privacy-page sentence that ASSERTED the bounded form ('usually within a few minutes') was removed with the page on 2026-08-29, so no shipped copy contradicts this record any more.

accepted_deviations.summary: The kind-30443 `d` slot id is a public, per-account coordinate every relay serving that account's KeyPackages can read. mint_d draws 32 bytes (64 hex chars), the width the Nostr transport binding fixes; builds before that fix drew 16 (32 hex chars), and THE BINDING MAKES THAT MALFORMED, NOT MERELY NARROW: `d` is 'exactly one tag, exactly one 64-character lowercase hex value decoding to 32 bytes', and 'if a required singleton tag is missing, repeated, has no value, or has extra values beyond the one defined here, the event is malformed' (transports/nostr.md), while foundation/key-packages.md requires an inviter to 'reject malformed or incompatible candidates before selecting one'. THE INVITABILITY COST IS NOW CLOSED, NOT ACCEPTED: a one-time, crash-safe retirement (decide_kp_slot_retirement, run by maintain_key_package ahead of the ordinary decision; sentinel kp_slot_retirement_done_v1) re-publishes the SAME tracked package into a freshly minted conformant slot and, only after a relay OK-ACKS it, publishes one NIP-09 kind-5 deletion of the orphaned coordinate ('a' = 30443:<pubkey>:<old d>, plus the observed id as 'e' and k=30443). Moving the same package rather than minting one keeps an in-flight Welcome against the retired coordinate decryptable, which holds for a tracked row whose lifetime is readable and non-empty; a dead or unreadable row is replaced by fresh material instead, and its superseded bytes are deleted once the replacement is acked. The sentinel latches only on a completed migration, so a failed publish, an unacked retraction or an unanswered probe resumes instead of latching — and an unacked retraction does not consume the tick either, so a relay that never acks a kind-5 cannot starve rotation, republish-if-missing and heal behind it. WHAT REMAINS ACCEPTED is the historical residue: NIP-09 deletion is advisory ('relays SHOULD delete'), so a relay that ignores the request — or that was unreachable while the migration ran and comes back serving the old event — can keep the 32-hex coordinate publicly readable, and no client can force its removal. That residue is an era marker (which build of Haven first published the account), not key material: the value is CSPRNG-random and non-derived (never from an account key, MLS leaf key, KeyPackageRef or device label). A lenient peer that still selects the orphan is not stranded where the package was MOVED — it carries the same one this device holds — until that package is next rotated or reaches Lifetime.not_after, the spec's own deletion bounds; where it had to be minted, the orphan advertises material the account no longer tracks, so such a peer can fail to invite it. Proofs: haven/rust_builder/src/api.rs tc8_a_pre_fix_install_is_retired_onto_a_conformant_slot_via_real_ffi, tc9_a_conformant_install_is_never_retired_via_real_ffi, tc10_no_retraction_until_the_replacement_is_acked_via_real_ffi, tc11_an_already_published_replacement_is_adopted_via_real_ffi, tc12_a_conformant_account_scrubs_a_leftover_orphan_via_real_ffi, tc13_a_refused_retraction_leaves_the_migration_open_via_real_ffi, tc14_a_never_acked_retraction_does_not_starve_rotation_via_real_ffi, tc15_an_unreadable_row_is_retired_onto_fresh_material_via_real_ffi; slot shape pinned by haven-core/tests/kp_rotation_e2e.rs::a_first_publish_mints_a_binding_shaped_random_slot_id.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not present the slot id as carrying nothing a relay can use, and must not claim that retiring the old slot ERASES it: NIP-09 deletion is a request relays SHOULD honour, so an old 32-hex coordinate can stay publicly readable on a relay that ignores it, identifying which era of Haven first published the account. Copy must equally not claim that every Haven account is invitable by any Marmot client the moment it is installed — the retirement needs one tick with a reachable KeyPackage relay to complete, and an account with no reachable relay is unreachable for ordinary reasons anyway. The id is random and reveals no key material.

avatarPickerPhotoRemoved.reason: Snackbar confirming the local removal action. Honest only because the confirmation dialog (photoHeaderRemoveBody) precedes it and states that the hosted image survives; on its own it must never read as a deletion promise. Its @description does not yet record this constraint.

locationDisclosureAgree.reason: Affirmative button label of the consent dialog. Records consent; asserts nothing about behaviour.

locationDisclosureNotNow.reason: Dismissal button label of the consent dialog. Declines consent; asserts nothing about behaviour.

locationDisclosureTitle.reason: Dialog heading ('Sharing your location'). Names the subject; every checkable claim lives in the why/how/sharing/background/manage paragraphs below it.

locationSettingsToggleSubtitle.reason: Toggle subtitle. Correct only by omission: it must describe the background scope without claiming sharing survives the system closing Haven, and is deliberately silent on the Android reboot/swipe-out asymmetry, which locationSettingsIntro states in full.

relaySettingsKeyPackageSubtitle.reason: Section subtitle naming where KeyPackage relays live. Correct only by omission: the profile plane moved to the separate local-only Profile list, so this line must stay silent about the public profile.

invariants.title: Location leaves the device only as MLS ciphertext
invariants.statement: Every coordinate that crosses the network boundary does so inside an MLS application message sealed by the group's exporter-derived key and framed as a kind-445 event; adding any publish path that writes a coordinate (or a geohash derived from one) into event content, a tag, or an HTTP body falsifies this.

event_kinds.note: Built by the rev-pinned peeler (transport-nostr-peeler/src/peeler.rs); reached from nostr/mls/manager.rs::send_location, which is the ONLY send path (a second one in location/nostr.rs was deleted 2026-08-14, having never had a caller). No repo-local grep can see the kind.

The inner application rumor carrying the coordinate, built at nostr/mls/manager.rs::location_rumor (the private helper nostr/mls/manager.rs::send_location delegates to). Never published as a relay event — it exists only as 445 plaintext before the engine seals it. It was kind 9 (the Marmot/White Noise CHAT kind) until 2026-08-24, which rendered Haven's location JSON as chat bubbles in any Marmot client sharing the circle; 25442 is drawn from the ephemeral band and is unallocated in the kind registry, the NIPs README, MDK and Haven. The token names a CONSTANT (KIND_LOCATION_UPDATE, haven-core/src/nostr/event.rs), so rule 13 can no longer see the number: the VALUE is pinned by scripts/ci/check_inner_location_kind.sh.

invariants.title: The location payload carries a coordinate and a timestamp, nothing else
invariants.statement: The serialized LocationMessage contains no device_id, altitude, speed, heading or raw_accuracy field even when those fields are populated in memory, and coordinates are full precision with no obfuscation tier to select; removing a serde(skip) or reintroducing a coarsening mode falsifies this.

event_kinds.note: The rumor whose JSON body this invariant constrains, built at nostr/mls/manager.rs::location_rumor, reached from ::send_location. The token names a CONSTANT, so rule 13 cannot see the number; scripts/ci/check_inner_location_kind.sh pins the value.

invariants.title: A co-member's non-location app event never becomes a map marker
invariants.statement: Haven's location updates travel under inner kind 25442 and never under the chat kind, and an inbound inner application event of any kind Haven does not own carries no content out of the receive gate — so it cannot place, move or attribute a member marker. The legacy chat kind is admitted only when paired with a ["t","location"] tag, the shape every Haven build through v0.1.12 emitted; dropping either half of that pairing, or gating on the tag alone, falsifies this.

event_kinds.note: The only inner kind Haven emits, built at nostr/mls/manager.rs::location_rumor. The receive gate (::is_location_rumor) admits it plus the legacy chat kind paired with a ["t","location"] tag. The token names a CONSTANT, so rule 13 cannot see the number; scripts/ci/check_inner_location_kind.sh pins the value and retires the legacy arm when the MDK pin moves.

invariants.title: No coordinate is produced after location access is withdrawn

invariants.title: Only Best-profile iOS fixes ever become a published coordinate
invariants.statement: On iOS the session runs at one of exactly two accuracy tiers, and only a fix delivered under the Best profile — desiredAccuracy == kCLLocationAccuracyBest AND computed after the switch to it (the bestSince comparison) — is emitted to Dart, cached as the publish input, or returned as last-known. A kCLLocationAccuracyHundredMeters fix serves the stationary/movement detector and the freshness bound and nothing else; it never reaches a subscriber, the motion trigger or the relay. A live session holds that fix THREE times — the native lastBestFix, the location service's _lastStreamPosition, and the profile controller's anchor — and all three clear together, on stream cancel, on a toggle-off pause, on logout and on an observed access loss, so no full-precision coordinate outlives the session in any of them. The last-known read is age-bounded by the same freshness rule as the cache read, so the fix one rejects as stale is not served by the other. Emitting or caching a 100 m-tier fix, dropping the bestSince comparison, adding a third accuracy value, serving the native cache unbounded, or clearing fewer than all three copies, each falsifies this. That freshness rule is itself bounded in TIME. A coarse-tier confirmation may extend how long the Best anchor is served past its own timestamp, but never beyond kStationaryAnchorMaxAge (5 min), enforced in two places: IosProfileController escalates to Best at that age however many coarse fixes have confirmed the anchor, and _streamFixIsFresh refuses to serve a fix older than it whatever the confirmation says. A published location carries the instant of the PUBLISH and never the fix time, so without that cap a stationary backgrounded device would re-publish one anchor indefinitely and a peer would read "just now" for a coordinate hours old and up to 200 m wrong. Removing either half of the cap, or measuring it from the confirmation rather than from the anchor's own timestamp, falsifies this too.

invariants.title: A circle that can no longer send is detected and named as that circle, and no background burst creates one
invariants.statement: Two halves, each falsifiable on its own. (a) A BACKGROUND burst never publishes a removal-bearing auto-commit — a departing peer's eviction, the only commit a receive path stages: under `ReceiveAutoCommitPolicy::DeferToForeground` the commit is parked as a durable per-circle row (`deferred_removal_commits`, written BEFORE the in-memory park) and is neither published nor rolled back, so no burst opens a publish-before-apply window the OS may end mid-flight; the FOREGROUND pass that redeems it keeps the obligation owed and retries when no relay acks, because a rollback is a permanent, silent drop of the removal at the pinned MDK rev and would leave the departed peer deriving the circle's keys. No plane anywhere rolls one back and no plane publishes one without first recording the obligation: the fail rung (`CircleManager::publish_failed`) keeps a removal-bearing commit staged and owed for every caller, in Rust and across the FFI, and every plane records the obligation write-ahead (`CircleManager::owe_removal_publish`). (b) A circle that can no longer send — the engine's terminal `Unrecoverable` verdict, or a parked eviction whose session died — is reported as its OWN per-circle `LiveSyncEvent::GroupUnrecoverable` naming the pseudonymous `nostr_group_id` and never the MLS group id, crossing the FFI as the additive nullable `unrecoverableNostrGroupId`. Publishing a removal-bearing auto-commit from a burst, rolling a parked one back, rolling one back from ANY plane, publishing one without first recording the obligation, redeeming one anywhere but a foreground open, flattening the verdict back into the per-event, self-clearing `SyncStatusReason::Unprocessable` (which names no circle), or putting the real MLS group id on the event falsifies this.

event_kinds.note: The eviction auto-commit is a kind-445 control message (h tag, no expiration), built by the rev-pinned peeler. This invariant is about WHEN it is put on the wire: never from a background burst, always from a foreground pass, and never abandoned. A parked commit is a 445 this device owes and has not sent.

invariants.residual: The verdict is now CONSUMED, and what is left is narrower than the statement rather than absent from it. `LiveEventRouter._handleStatus` reads `unrecoverableNostrGroupId` BEFORE its null-reason early return, resolves the circle and marks it blocked (`markCircleBlocked`), which is what disables that circle's send and mutate affordances and raises the circle-details blocked banner; the banner names the circle and offers a re-create that opens the create flow with this circle's display name pre-filled and touches the broken group not at all, so the cached roster and last-known locations stay readable beneath it. NO ARB KEY WAS ADDED: the affordance reuses `legacyCircleRecreateCta`, already present in all thirteen locales, because a template key missing from a shipped locale is a RED gate here (`l10n.yaml`'s `untranslated-messages-file` plus step 1 of `check_l10n_parity.sh`), so an English-only string could not have landed at all. This entry still declares no `assertion_arb_keys`, and that is deliberate rather than leftover: its promise is that the wedge is DETECTED and NAMED per circle, not any particular sentence of copy, and the strings the banner renders are the pre-existing blocked-circle copy rather than new claims of this invariant. WHAT THE CONSUMER COSTS, and it is user-visible. The mark needs TWO observations of the same circle in DIFFERENT re-anchor generations — counted off the `SyncStatusReason::BackgroundResumed` marker on the same ordered stream, never off a clock, so there is no timer and no wall-clock assumption — because ONE verdict has a documented false positive: the report sweep runs immediately after a re-anchor subscribes and can race a remaining peer's healing commit, and telling a user to rebuild a circle that works costs them the whole roster's invitations. So the banner appears on the SECOND foreground open, not the first. That is the same horizon as the repair itself — a foreground open is also the only place a parked eviction is published — so the delay costs no recovery, only the announcement. Three limits of the detection itself, all argued at `report_unrecoverable_circles`: a circle a remaining peer ALREADY HEALED can be reported once, because at MDK `e391adc` no read accessor reveals a staged commit and the row is discharged only by the next successful publish (`discharge_removal_deferral_after_send`); a device wedged by a session that PREDATES this code carries no durable row and is undetectable by construction; and the verdict is evaluated only on a foreground re-anchor, never at `start`, which cannot tell a foreground launch from a background wake that cold-launched the process. Half (a)'s SUPPRESSION is scoped to the live-sync burst plane, but its two supporting guarantees are now tree-wide: no plane rolls a removal-bearing auto-commit back (the decision lives at `CircleManager::publish_failed`, the one rung the four planes share, so it binds the two that resolve the commit from Dart too), and every plane records the obligation BEFORE it opens the publish-before-apply window (`CircleManager::owe_removal_publish`), so a wake window the OS ends mid-publish leaves a durable row the next foreground live-sync open reports — on that plane; see the poll-configuration paragraph at the end of this residual for the build where no such open exists. The Android background catch-up sweep still PUBLISHES rather than parking, and that reason is now recorded at the call site and asserted by tests: a park needs somewhere to be redeemed and a `PendingStateRef` is valid only inside the session that staged it, so a sweep driven from a background isolate could never publish what it parked. What remains open is redemption ACROSS a session: an obligation the foreground service or the WorkManager catch-up worker records is reported but not redeemable, because at MDK `e391adc` nothing can re-derive a staged eviction from group state. Such a wedge is therefore LOUD AND TERMINAL — named to the user, repaired only by re-creating the circle — which is strictly better than the silent permanent drop it replaced, and is not a heal. And half (a)'s own cost is disclosed to nobody, because a LIVE parked eviction is deliberately not reported (only an orphaned one is): while it stands, that circle's `encrypt_location` fails the engine's "send requires Stable" gate until the next foreground re-anchor, which on a rarely-foregrounded device is a real per-circle gap in that circle's sharing. FINALLY, BOTH HALVES ARE LIVE-SYNC-SHAPED, and the retained poll rollback path (`HAVEN_LIVE_SYNC=false`) reaches NEITHER: `redeem_removal_deferrals` and `report_unrecoverable_circles` are invoked from one place only in production code (their own unit tests aside), a FOREGROUND burst open in `relay/live_sync/session.rs`, and a flag-off build starts no session at all. An unacked publish on that plane therefore records an obligation nothing will ever redeem, and the circle it wedges gets no per-circle `GroupUnrecoverable` verdict, so the blocked banner never names it. This is NOT a weakening of either half: the obligation is still written ahead of the window and still never rolled back, the pre-deferral behaviour dropped the removal outright, the flag-independent sharing-health banner still reports the silence, and a circle whose own decrypt returns `Unrecoverable` is still marked blocked through `_convertLocationEventResult` on either plane. What is absent on the poll plane is the parked-obligation half of the naming, and it is recorded as an open owner question (`docs/POWER_EFFICIENCY_PLAN.md` §9.9) rather than fixed here, because the three answers — redeem on the poll plane, name it there another way, or accept it — are a product decision.

invariants.title: Each circle is an independent MLS group with its own keys
invariants.statement: Two circles never share key material or a group identifier, and ciphertext produced in one circle is undecryptable by a member of another even when that member is in both; deriving any circle's keys from a shared or account-level secret falsifies this.

event_kinds.note: The per-circle ciphertext whose cross-group undecryptability this invariant asserts.

invariants.title: MLS signing keys are never the Nostr identity key
invariants.statement: The MLS leaf signature key and the Nostr identity key can never be the same key, structurally: ciphersuite 0x0001 fixes the leaf signature scheme to Ed25519 while the Nostr identity is secp256k1 Schnorr. The account-identity proof does NOT enforce inequality — validate_leaf_account_identity_proof authenticates the binding (a proof binding a key to itself would verify) — so the engine rejecting an unverifiable proof is not what makes this true.

event_kinds.note: Built by AccountIdentityProofRequest::proof_event() in cgka-engine, reached from the IN-TREE call site haven-core/src/nostr/mls/signer.rs. NOT the peeler. Never published. Note the shipped code (v2 / 0xF2F1 / kind-450-framed) diverges from foundation/account-identity-proof-v1.md, which specifies v0x01 and says the proof is not a Nostr event at all — a spec catch-up would be a wire-format change.

invariants.title: Every kind-445 carries a fresh, single-use author key
invariants.statement: Each group message is signed by a newly generated keypair, so no two location events share an author pubkey and none of them is the sender's identity key; reusing a keypair across messages, or letting the exporter-derived ChaCha20-Poly1305 nonce repeat under one epoch key, falsifies this.

event_kinds.note: wire_allowlist.json marks this kind ephemeral_pubkey:true, which the wire-journal oracle enforces on real published events.

invariants.title: Keys change on membership change or an explicit repair, never on a timer
invariants.statement: Both periodic (MIP-03 SHOULD) and post-join 24 h (MIP-02 MUST) leaf-key self-update are disabled, so one epoch key can cover weeks of messages and a former member keeps whatever they saved during their epochs. At code level several admin commits advance an epoch (a membership change, a relay-list update via update_circle_relays, and each half of an admin handoff). What a USER can reach today is two: changing who is in a circle, and - if they are its sole admin - tapping Repair on a circle whose delivery has broken (Unit E, docs/EPOCH_ROTATION_REPAIR_PLAN.md), which is rate-limited to once per circle per 24 h and reachable only from the foreground service layer. That user-reachable scoping was what the Privacy-page copy described until the page was removed on 2026-08-29; it is now recorded here and in SECURITY.md (M5) only, and a screen that lets a user edit a circle's relays would add a third and MUST revisit this statement. The absolute half of this invariant is unchanged: NOTHING re-keys on a timer. Re-introducing a production self-update timer, or making the repair schedulable, would change that property; scripts/ci/check_epoch_repair_isolation.sh and haven/test/lints/self_update_disabled_test.dart both enforce that it stays user-triggered and foreground-only.

invariants.title: Removing a member advances the epoch and locks them out of new location
invariants.statement: An ADMIN removal is a commit that advances the group epoch, and a member removed at epoch N cannot decrypt a location published at epoch N+1; the commit is applied only after at least one relay acked it, so a member is never treated as removed on a commit nobody received.

event_kinds.note: Removal commits ride the same kind as application messages, distinguished only by the absence of the expiration tag.

The SELF-LEAVE path (which the Privacy-page sentence covered until the page was removed on 2026-08-29) has an accepted unconverged case (deviation LEAVE-GHOST) where the ghost stays authorized until a manual admin removal; that removal is now an affordance an admin actually has (the member row's remove button, shipped 2026-08-15), where before it existed only as a service with no caller. Nothing still fails when the self-leave path breaks, and since 2026-08-29 no copy describes it either way; LEAVE-GHOST stays a registered deviation without an invariant of its own (docs/privacy/README.md, Known gaps). circleMemberRemoveDialogBody makes the forward-secrecy claim in the admin's own words and circleMemberRemoveError makes the rollback one; both are backed by the tests above, but neither is reachable by the claim-language sweep, so this row is what keeps them proven.

invariants.title: A joiner receives current-epoch keys only and no replayed history
invariants.statement: A member added at epoch N cannot DECRYPT any kind-445 sealed before the commit that added them, regardless of what a relay serves: the Welcome conveys only the current epoch's joiner_secret path and the MLS key schedule is one-way, so no earlier exporter_secret is derivable. Haven additionally has no backfill path — the Add stages no application message and the welcome ingest carries no location results.
invariants.note: Delivery of pre-join ciphertext to a joiner is REACHABLE and harmless: SEED_LOOKBACK_SECS = 86_400 (relay/live_sync/session.rs:54) seeds a new circle's kind-445 cursor to now-24h rather than to the join epoch, so the first sweep's REQ window legitimately covers up to a day before the join. The 228 s NIP-40 expiration means a conformant relay holds almost nothing that old, but a buggy or hostile one may serve it. The claim holds because the ciphertext is UNREADABLE, not because it is never delivered — which is exactly what the cited test pins, by handing the joiner the real pre-join event through process_event.

invariants.title: Exactly five past epochs of exporter secrets are retained
invariants.statement: The engine keeps DEFAULT_MAX_PAST_EPOCHS = 5 past epochs' exporter secrets and its application-message accept window equals that bound, so a ciphertext exactly at the window edge still decrypts and one past it does not; widening the window keeps stale secrets alive, narrowing it drops legitimate offline backlog, and either direction fails the pin.

invariants.title: Every co-member learns your Nostr identity public key
invariants.statement: Each MLS leaf carries a kind-450 account-identity proof binding the member to their Nostr identity key, and the engine rejects a leaf whose proof does not verify, so joining a circle necessarily discloses that pubkey to every other member and to everyone already in the circle; there is no pseudonymous-within-circle mode.

event_kinds.note: Built by AccountIdentityProofRequest::proof_event() in cgka-engine, reached from the IN-TREE call site haven-core/src/nostr/mls/signer.rs. NOT the peeler. Never published. Note the shipped code (v2 / 0xF2F1 / kind-450-framed) diverges from foundation/account-identity-proof-v1.md, which specifies v0x01 and says the proof is not a Nostr event at all — a spec catch-up would be a wire-format change.

invariants.title: A kind-445 carries h and expiration and no other tag
invariants.statement: Published group events carry only the h routing tag (plus a NIP-40 expiration on application messages); no alt tag, no geohash g tag and no client tag ever reaches a relay — in particular the dead local 445 builder at nostr/event.rs, which stamps alt and a truncated 5-char geohash, must stay unreachable.

event_kinds.note: wire_allowlist.json pins tags.allowed = [h, expiration] and tags.required = [h, expiration]; a geohash or alt tag landing on the wire is a violation.
Read-side subscription filter for the group plane (live_sync/planes/group.rs:14) — same kind, spelled as a numeric literal rather than reached through the peeler.

invariants.title: Every kind-445 application message this device publishes carries a NIP-40 expiry of at most 228 s; control messages carry none
invariants.statement: Every kind-445 APPLICATION message THIS DEVICE publishes carries a NIP-40 `expiration` of inner_created_at + at most LOCATION_MESSAGE_RETENTION_SECS (228 s), in EVERY circle — including one created by a client that declared no message-retention.v1 component (0x8005), where the engine would stamp nothing: the installed peeler (RetentionBoundPeeler) supplies Haven's own window when the group declares none or zero, caps a longer group policy to it, and honours a shorter one as declared. This device never stamps a commit or proposal, so among the 445s THIS device sends, the absence of an expiration identifies a group-control message. That inference does NOT extend to the circle's whole #h stream: in a circle declaring no component, another member's unstamped 445 may be a location update (see residual). The tag set on this device's 445s is exactly `h` for control and `h` + `expiration` for application messages — nothing else.

event_kinds.note: The engine derives the expiration from the group component; Haven's send path takes no per-send expiration.
Welcome gift wraps carry no expiration — the invitation may sit on an inbox relay indefinitely.

invariants.residual: Bounded to the traffic THIS device authors, which is all it can bound. In a circle created by a client that declared no 0x8005 component, another member's own location 445s still carry no expiration: they may be retained indefinitely AND, to any relay watching the circle's public #h, they are indistinguishable from membership changes — so in such a mixed circle the un-stamped class contains another member's LOCATION UPDATES, not only control messages. The un-stamped class is every group-control message, not membership alone — an admin handoff and a relay-set change are UpdateAppComponents commits and are un-stamped too, which is what `expiration_separates_location_from_control_and_no_other_tag_appears` actually publishes. The Privacy-page sentence that stated this discriminator (scoped to the messages this device sends) was removed with the page on 2026-08-29; SECURITY.md's discriminator bullet is now its only statement. Haven still cannot repair the group itself: writing the component is admin-gated upstream (require_admin on the UpdateAppComponents path) and a joiner is not an admin, and doing it inside the join path would stage an epoch-advancing commit whose non-publication pins the group in PendingPublish and buffers every inbound message forever, which is a worse loss than the leak. The residue is disclosed nowhere: nothing in the app tells the user that in such a circle another member's location 445s may sit on a relay indefinitely and read as group control — and since the owner removed the in-app explanation layer on 2026-08-29 there is no surface left to disclose it on, so it is recorded in SECURITY.md rather than held open as a copy decision. SECOND: the bound MASKS the group-level declaration, and it masks it in three pre-existing proofs, not one. `encrypt_location_attaches_group_retention_expiration` and `decrypt_location_drops_expired_event` (src/circle/manager.rs) and the E2E wire oracle (tooling/e2e/wire_allowlist.json, kind 445 `required: [h, expiration]`) all now pass with create_group's 0x8005 declaration removed, because the bound supplies the tag they look for; `live_sync_cursor_replay_e2e.rs`'s expiration precondition is masked the same way. NOTHING AT THE WIRE LEVEL still proves Haven declares 0x8005 to its peers, and the component is the only thing governing every OTHER member's client. Held at host level instead, by `a_locally_created_circle_declares_havens_retention_window_to_every_member` (both parties read the window back out of group state) and `a_shorter_group_policy_reaches_the_wire_as_declared` (a foreign circle's narrower window reaches the wire as declared, which the bound could not fake). Closing it on the wire needs an allow-list entry that asserts the delta VALUE against the circle's declared window rather than the tag's presence — owned by the E2E lane, not by this crate. THIRD: the bound honours an arbitrarily short declared window, so a circle whose creator declares e.g. 1 s has every Haven member's location dropped by a NIP-40-honouring relay almost immediately. Deliberately not floored — a floor would ask relays to hold location ciphertext LONGER than the circle declared, and would not restore visibility, since the same component governs every other member's client. SECURITY.md's no-gap invariant is scoped to circles Haven created for exactly this reason — and, since PUB-COALESCE, to rosters of at most kMaxCirclesPerBurst circles as well — which is every roster the app admits, because kMaxCirclesPerAccount (10) refuses the eleventh (INV-W-445-EXPIRATION-WINDOW). That window is no longer undisclosed: the circle-details subtitle reports the EFFECTIVE window for the messages this device sends into that circle — in seconds when it is under a minute, so a narrow foreign window reads as alarming rather than being rounded away — held by INV-U-CIRCLE-EXPIRY-SHOWN-IS-EXPIRY-SENT. What the sheet does not say is WHY it is short: it reports the number, not that another client chose it.

invariants.title: The relay-residency window Haven asks for is the CEILING the copy states, and the smallest the no-gap floor allows — at every roster the account bound admits
invariants.statement: LOCATION_MESSAGE_RETENTION_SECS is the CEILING on the NIP-40 window Haven requests, not the window every message carries: an application kind-445 gets it whenever the group declares no message-retention.v1 (0x8005) window, declares zero, or declares a LONGER one, while a SHORTER declared window is honoured as declared (bounded_retention_secs — see INV-W-445-EXPIRATION-SCOPE for the per-message rule and INV-U-CIRCLE-EXPIRY-SHOWN-IS-EXPIRY-SENT for what the user is shown). The constant equals kLocationPublishMaxInterval + 2 * kTtlNetworkBufferSeconds read out of haven/lib/src/constants/location.dart. Three things therefore move together: the no-widening bound (a larger window leaves every published location on relays longer than the design commits to), the no-narrowing bound (a smaller one leaves a member returning from offline with nothing unexpired left to fetch), and the honouring of a shorter declared window (a flat figure would be false in every circle another client created with a narrower window, which is the circle whose window the user cannot change; the wire-level proof is INV-W-445-EXPIRATION-SCOPE's a_shorter_group_policy_reaches_the_wire_as_declared, and the effective figure the user still sees is the circle-details subtitle, INV-U-CIRCLE-EXPIRY-SHOWN-IS-EXPIRY-SENT). The Privacy-page sentence that quoted the figure ('about four minutes', as an 'at most' bound) was removed with the page on 2026-08-29 and its copy-tie tests with it; SECURITY.md carries the derivation. Editing the constant, the Dart publish ceiling, or the honouring of a shorter declared window without the others fails. The no-gap floor the ceiling is sized against is a bound on the SCHEDULED gap and it holds for rosters up to kMaxCirclesPerBurst (11): one coalesced burst per interval publishes every eligible circle (PUB-COALESCE), so a circle that leads one burst and trails the next waits kLocationPublishMaxInterval (168 s) plus at most one burst spread (kPublishStaggerMaxSpread, 30 s) = 198 s, leaving the whole 30 s of kTtlNetworkBufferSeconds unspent. From the twelfth circle up the burst would defer its tail and that floor would no longer hold, which is why the ROSTER is bounded below the burst cap: kMaxCirclesPerAccount (10) refuses circle creation and invitation accept — the only two operations that CREATE a circles row — at the one seam both reach the core through, so the floor holds at every roster a user can have and the ceil(N / kMaxCirclesPerBurst) service-period ladder is unreachable in production. What this entry does NOT promise is the propagation margin its predecessor had: the burst spread spends one of the two kTtlNetworkBufferSeconds, so the margin is 30 s and not 60 s at every roster from two circles up, and the residual says so — as it does for the three REALIZED-gap terms that sit outside this SCHEDULED bound, TWO of which cross the retention at rosters this bound admits.

invariants.residual: The no-gap property this constant is sized for is a bound on the SCHEDULED gap, and it is bounded by the ROSTER at eleven circles — which is why the roster itself is bounded at TEN. kMaxCirclesPerAccount (owner decision, 2026-09-09) refuses circle creation and invitation accept once the account holds ten accepted circles, enforced in NostrCircleService because its two roster-growing calls are the only Dart callers of the only two core operations that CREATE a circles row: create_circle_with_config, which upserts through CircleStorage::save_circle, and record_processed_invitation, which runs its own INSERT INTO circles. 'CREATE' and not 'write' is the property, and the difference is load-bearing rather than pedantic: save_circle is an UPSERT with three further non-test callers (resync_circle_relays_from_mdk, add_members, remove_members), and record_processed_invitation is not among them; each of those three reads the row back with storage.get_circle first and returns early when there is none, so none of them can mint one. The gate is also enforced against CONCURRENCY, not only against call sites: _refuseIfRosterFull RESERVES the admitted slot (_reservedRosterSlots, released in the caller's finally), because the row only exists once the core write returns, so without the reservation simultaneous accepts would each read the same pre-growth roster and enough of them would carry it past kMaxCirclesPerBurst — the deferral the bound exists to eliminate. The call-site half is pinned by 'only the gated service grows the account roster' (haven/test/lints/circle_roster_bound_sites_test.dart), an AST inventory over all of lib minus lib/src/rust/ — main.dart included, with its own anti-vacuity assertion — which fails on a third call site rather than letting one land silently; the concurrency half by 'admit exactly one when only one slot is left' and its two slot-release siblings. A burst is therefore never handed more than ten circles and the deferral ladder below is UNREACHABLE in production. THE LADDER IS KEPT ON RECORD BECAUSE THE DEFERRAL CODE IS, and lifting the bound re-opens it verbatim: a burst publishes at most kMaxCirclesPerBurst (11) circles and defers the rest to the next tick, _takeBurstSlice is strict round-robin, so a DEFERRED circle's worst SERVICE PERIOD would be ceil(N / 11) bursts rather than two at every roster — N = 12..22 -> TWO sampled intervals (144 s best, 240 s mean, 336 s worst, and 366 s once the burst-position differential is added, because a circle may lead one burst and trail the one two ticks later, a whole kPublishStaggerMaxSpread apart); N = 23..33 -> three (216 / 360 / 504 s); N >= 34 -> four or more, where even the BEST case (288 s) exceeds the 228 s retention on EVERY publish rather than on some. Both halves stay PINNED rather than left as prose, so that a lifted bound cannot re-open them unmeasured: the round-robin period by 'a deferred circle waits ceil(N / kMaxCirclesPerBurst) bursts' (which drives real ticks through _takeBurstSlice, so it fails when the slice size or the rotate moves) and the seconds by 'and past the cap, the deferral ladder in SECONDS' (which reads them off the cadence constants, so it fails when the cadence moves). The two scope limits that used to matter go with it: a tick folding into a running iOS burst (BackgroundBurstCoordinator._joinable), and the 21-circle point where a one-shot's own spread outlasts kLocationPublishOverlapGuard, are both reachable only at N >= 12. WHAT THE BOUND DOES NOT CLOSE, and what this entry therefore does not promise. FIRST, the PROPAGATION MARGIN. Against the ACTUAL predecessor — per-circle schedulers, where the gap was each circle's own sampled interval, <= 168 s at every N, with no spread and no deferral — the full 60 s (2 x kTtlNetworkBufferSeconds) was margin; since PUB-COALESCE the burst spread spends one of the two, so this invariant runs on 30 s of propagation and clock-skew margin at every roster from TWO circles up. That halving is not a past-eleven effect and the roster bound does not touch it; it is recorded in the ratchet_override block for PUB-COALESCE, the change that caused it, so it sits in a reviewed diff and not only here. SECOND, the period is a period of TURNS, and a turn is a SELECTION rather than a publish: the rotation advances when the tick FIRES, ahead of the chain, the window and the sink, so a slice that loses its window (no identity, disclosure not accepted, a fix that timed out, a pause under it, an iOS coordinator that drops a queued burst) publishes nothing and waits a whole interval over again — up to 336 s against this 228 s retention, at every roster including a bounded one. The health model is told; the queue is not. THIRD, THREE REALIZED-gap terms sit outside this SCHEDULED bound, and two of them cross the retention at rosters the bound admits. The Android foreground service publishes on a platform delivery that arrives a TTFF late: on API 23-30 a cold acquisition reaches 248 s, i.e. 20 s past this 228 s, pinned by equality per API regime in haven/test/services/background_fix_request_test.dart. The iOS burst HEAD (connect, backlog wait and one-shot fix, up to 40 s) varies between bursts and so enters the realized gap as a differential on top of the spread: 168 + 40 + spread reaches 235 s at four circles and 238 s from five up, so iOS is inside 228 s only up to three circles. The THIRD is the only one that scales with N and coalescing introduced it: the pass is SERIAL and the stagger buys separation on top of each publish rather than inside it, so the foreground _pacedPublish — which measures the gap from the previous publish's START — spans sum(max(gap_i, dur_i)), while the background pass awaits the gap AFTER the previous publish returns and is strictly additive, sum(dur_i + gap_i+1); at one publish priced at kBurstPublishBudget (10 s) the realized span reaches about 100 s (foreground shape) or 130 s (background) against a SCHEDULED 30 s spread, and it lands twice — once in a realized gap and once in the duration-shaped circle-count estimator PUB-COALESCE records. So this entry is a promise about the SCHEDULE at every reachable roster, and must not be read as 'a peer's marker never expires': on iOS with background sharing on it CAN expire before the replacement lands, from FOUR circles up, which is an ordinary roster and not a corner. All three are stated on haven/lib/src/constants/location.dart, and their PROOF status differs, which is the reason to state it: only the Android 248 s is pinned, by equality per API regime (haven/test/services/background_fix_request_test.dart, 'a cold TTFF outruns the lead, and on API ≤ 30 it outruns the retention as well — the residual, exactly'). The iOS 235/238 s crossing and the 100/130 s serial span are arithmetic over kBurstConnectBudget, kBurstBacklogBudget, kBurstWindowBudget, kBurstPublishBudget and the stagger that NO test asserts — burstBound pins the composition of those budgets, never the seconds they add up to — so those two are DISCLOSED and not enforced, and moving a budget moves them silently. THE ROTATION FACTS THAT MAKE THE PERIOD ABSOLUTE ARE UNCHANGED and still worth stating, because they are what keeps a lost turn from compounding: _rotation outlives stopScheduling()/startScheduling() and outlives an emission reporting nothing eligible (circlesProvider degrades ANY roster-read failure to an empty list, so an empty emission is at least as often a transient FFI/keyring error as a real departure), so neither a backgrounding nor a failed roster read re-phases whose turn it is — pinned by 'a deferred circle is not deferred again by every resume', 'a transient empty roster emission does not re-phase whose turn it is' and 'a roster change keeps survivors' places in the queue', and structurally by scripts/ci/check_publish_rotation_fairness.sh, which pins _rotation.clear() to exactly ONE site inside build() and the survivor merge to below the _circles.isEmpty guard. What DOES rewind the queue is build() — a fresh container, or the invalidate in IdentityNotifier.deleteIdentity — and a process restart, which does not persist it; and because the roster keeps filterPublishEligibleCircles order (getVisibleCircles() orders by updated_at DESC) a rewind returns to the SAME head and re-serves the same first slice, a deterministic re-service and not a re-phase. At a bounded roster the first slice IS the roster, so a rewind serves all of it.

invariants.title: The routing tag is a pseudonym, and Haven never rotates it
invariants.statement: Published events carry nostr_group_id in the h tag and the real MLS group ID appears nowhere in the event JSON or any tag; the tag is stable for the life of a circle because Haven never invokes the rotation the nostr-routing component permits, so a relay can group one circle's traffic indefinitely. Publishing the raw MLS group ID, or leaving the copy attributing the stability to the protocol rather than to Haven, falsifies this.

event_kinds.note: h tag carries nostr_group_id.
The welcome gift wrap must also not leak the raw MLS group ID.

invariants.residual: Component presence is the invariant, NOT engine behaviour. cgka-engine's transport_group_id_of_group falls back to the RAW MLS GroupId when a group carries no NostrRoutingV1 (0x8004) component, and that value is what the peeler hex-encodes into the h tag — a direct Security Rule 4 violation with no engine-side refusal. Haven is safe today for two incidental reasons, neither tested: create_circle always mints the component, and accept_invitation fails closed if a joined group lacks routing. Residual path: an admin co-member clearing the component via UpdateAppComponents on an existing circle. encrypt_location reads circle.nostr_group_id from STORAGE for publish targeting while the h tag comes from the ENGINE at wrap time, and nothing cross-checks the two. The cited test exercises only a Haven-created group with an intact component, so it cannot see this.

invariants.title: Invitations travel as unsigned rumors inside gift wraps with fresh authors
invariants.statement: The kind-444 Welcome rumor carries no signature (so a recipient cannot republish it as the inviter), it is delivered inside a NIP-59 kind-1059 gift wrap authored by a freshly generated key, and neither the wrap nor its tags leak the MLS group ID, the circle name or the roster; signing the rumor, reusing a wrap author, or adding any tag beyond p falsifies this.

invariants.title: The expiry a circle's details sheet shows is the expiry this device stamps on its own location messages
invariants.statement: The circle-details subtitle reports the EFFECTIVE relay-retention window for the location messages THIS device sends into that circle — bounded_retention_secs applied to the group's declared 0x8005 component — and never the raw declaration. The two diverge in exactly the cases that matter: a circle that declares nothing, and one that declares longer than Haven's own window, both collapse to LOCATION_MESSAGE_RETENTION_SECS, while a SHORTER foreign declaration is honoured and is therefore shown as declared. A circle with no live MLS group shows no window at all rather than falling back to Haven's, because the fallback would report 'about four minutes' for a circle that cannot send. The copy states whose messages the number governs ('the location updates you send') and keeps the window a request to relays rather than a promise of deletion.

invariants.title: The inbox and KeyPackage relay lists are published under the identity key
invariants.statement: Haven publishes a kind-10050 inbox relay list and a kind-10002 NIP-65 list, both signed by the identity key and both fanned out to the relays already on them, and it publishes kind-30443 KeyPackages to those relays; consequently every URL a user adds to those lists becomes public and permanently linked to their pubkey, and the retired kind-10051 is emitted only as an empty replaceable retraction.

invariants.title: No wire kind exists for the profile relay category
invariants.statement: RelayType::Profile::to_kind() returns None, so there is no kind an EventBuilder could be handed for a profile relay list and no code path can serialize that list into a published event; a relay that only carries location or invitation traffic therefore has no signed pointer telling it which relays the device uses for its profile. Adding a kind mapping, or publishing a kind-10002 that names the profile pool, falsifies this.
