invariants.title: Haven operates no server of its own on any plane
invariants.statement: There is no Haven-operated relay, no Haven backend, and no account record: the seeded relays are third-party Nostr relays, identity creation takes no email, phone number or password, and the map plane's only first-party artefact is a single shared Stadia API key carrying no per-user identifier. Introducing a Haven-hosted endpoint that receives user data falsifies this.

invariants.title: No push notification plane exists
invariants.statement: No FCM/APNs/OneSignal-class dependency is declared in pubspec.yaml, and nothing under haven/ios registers for remote notifications (no remote-notification background mode, no aps-environment entitlement, no registerForRemoteNotifications), so no coordinator ever learns when someone in a circle has something to deliver.

invariants.title: No analytics, crash-reporting or advertising code ships
invariants.statement: The app declares no analytics, crash-reporting or ad SDK and contains no code path that reports usage, exceptions or identifiers to any third party; adding a Sentry/Crashlytics/Firebase-Analytics-class dependency, or a hand-rolled event-reporting HTTP call, falsifies this.
invariants.note: Backed by check 9b of that guard — the analytics/crash-reporting/advertising dependency surface, the sibling of check 9's push ban. Refuses such a dependency in every position that reaches a build (pubspec direct AND dev, the transitive pubspec.lock, both Cargo manifests and lockfiles, every haven/android build file, AndroidManifest components, Info.plist keys, PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy, a Podfile when present, and marker config files whose presence alone is an SDK). It cannot see a hand-rolled http.post of usage data, an SDK vendored inside another plugin's native artifact, or a Gradle coordinate assembled from variables.

invariants.title: More than one relay is seeded, so no single relay can cut a user off
invariants.statement: PRODUCTION_DEFAULT_RELAYS holds exactly three wss:// relays run by independent operators, and no relay in that set is Haven-operated or individually required; shrinking the set to one — or to two, which is thinner than the copy discloses — falsifies the "several relays, so no single one can cut you off" promise.

invariants.title: A circle's relay set comes from the invitees, not from the creator's list
invariants.statement: create_circle uses the relays supplied by the invited members' fetched KeyPackages; only when that union is empty does it fall back to the creator's stored inbox relays, and only when those are also empty does it fall back to the built-in defaults. Restoring a "copied from your inbox relays" derivation would make the circle-details note false in the normal case.

invariants.title: The live-sync engine never authenticates and never fans out beyond the configured relays
invariants.statement: The engine Client is built with automatic_authentication(false) and no gossip, so it refuses every NIP-42 AUTH challenge (never signing a kind-22242 that would join the identity key to the circle traffic on that socket) and its relay pool equals exactly the configured circle-union-inbox set even after a kind-10002 advertises a phantom relay. verify_subscriptions must also stay off, or fresh REQs silently drop their first stored events.

event_kinds.note: Read-side: a kind-10002 advertising a phantom relay must not expand the engine's pool.

NIP-42 AUTH. Haven never signs one — build_engine_client sets automatic_authentication(false). Declared so the kind-based closed world can see the one kind whose appearance would falsify this invariant.

invariants.title: The publish relay pool sends no keepalives and closes between bursts
invariants.statement: Every RelayManager publish pool — the UI isolate's, the Android foreground service's, and any other isolate that builds one — registers each relay through RelayPool::add_relay with publish_relay_options(): ping(false), so no WebSocket keepalive frame leaves the device between publish bursts; sleep_when_idle(true) with a 10 s idle timeout, so the socket closes within roughly a minute of the last publish rather than being held open; and reconnect(false), because the idle monitor runs only inside a live connection task, so a dropped socket that kept reconnecting would never reach Sleeping. Client::add_relay must never be used on that pool: for a URL the pool already holds it ORs RelayServiceFlags::default() (READ | WRITE | PING) onto the live relay and silently restores the keepalive on every socket. Every RelayManager fetch primitive leaves no subscription registered behind it, so nothing holds the socket awake after a fetch. The ENGINE pool (build_engine_client) deliberately KEEPS the pool's ping, because it holds standing REQs and carries no other traffic: turning it off there re-creates the dead-but-running relay blackout that nothing notices until the 15-minute health tick.

invariants.title: Backgrounded on iOS, presence is revealed only at publish instants
invariants.statement: While backgrounded on iOS with background sharing ON, from the completion of the pause branch's teardown until the next burst's open, the live-sync engine holds no standing subscription and no socket IT ASKED FOR: pause_subscriptions CLOSEs every REQ, sweeps any that a partial unsubscribe_all left registered (both bounded by RELAY_LIFECYCLE_OP_TIMEOUT and log-and-proceed on expiry), drains what is already downloaded through the Pause marker (note_delivery_gap, never a forget_*, so an un-applied hold-back survives; best-effort — on a dead worker or an unacked marker the router is cleared directly and the undrained backlog is re-downloaded by the next re-anchor), waits UNCAPPED for every in-flight publish (Security Rule 13), and only then terminates every relay through terminate_all_relays (client.disconnect(), re-read and re-asserted over RELAY_TERMINATE_ROUNDS rounds, never client.shutdown()), so that where the termination converges the crate's per-relay connection task and its 55 s pinger exit with it — see exception (iii) for where it does not. Each publish tick runs exactly one bounded burst instead: open_background_burst re-issues every REQ in the Resubscribe phase — each circle at its persisted cursor less GROUP_RESUBSCRIBE_BUFFER_SECS, and the inbox at INBOX_RESUBSCRIBE_LOOKBACK_SECS on every INBOX_BURSTS_PER_REQ-th background burst, never the cold-start window — waits up to BURST_BACKLOG_WAIT_SECS per (relay, subscription) endpoint for EOSE so a peer commit ingested here is APPLIED before the location is encrypted, publishes, folds due KeyPackage/relay-list maintenance onto the warm publish pool, settles (COMMIT_SETTLE_WINDOW_SECS from the last commit activity, capped by BURST_SETTLE_CAP_SECS, which bounds idle follow-on activity only and never an in-flight publish), pauses, drains any commit-critical publish still on the shared publish pool, and shuts that pool. A pause that drives no burst — nothing eligible, or a publish still inside kLocationPublishOverlapGuard — runs that same teardown on its own (closeIdle, on the same chain and under the same in-burst flag, so it can never run beside a burst), which is what makes the gap before the first burst no exception. THREE exception classes and one separate plane, all stated. (i) The teardown STOPS wherever the foreground reclaimed the engine, leaving the publish pool to the next pause's teardown. (ii) A cold launch whose un-awaited engine start completes after the teardown ran comes up Live in the background — bounded by the first tick's own teardown, and UNBOUNDED where no tick is coming: with no publish-eligible circle there is no per-circle tick, so nothing calls open_background_burst and nothing calls pause_subscriptions, and the engine holds every group REQ, the inbox #p REQ and its socket for the whole background window. (iii) The termination is a REPAIR PLUS A WATCH, never a prevention: nostr-relay-pool's own retry loop can re-open a REAL socket over the pause's Terminated and hold it with 55 s pings indefinitely (the race is inside the pinned crate, between two adjacent statements of InnerRelay::disconnect, so the engine cannot make it impossible), and non-convergence after RELAY_TERMINATE_ROUNDS warns with a COUNT only. What is promised instead is that no such socket SURVIVES — run_monitor's radio-off watch cuts every one, including the strand this loop cannot see at all (a Disconnected write that landed BEFORE the pool's Terminated store), and unrequested_connections is how many there were. The publish pool is a separate plane the burst does not own — the motion trigger may re-open it between bursts — and how it closes SPLITS BY PLANE, so no single claim covers all three. On this branch and on the Android foreground service it is closed COLLECTIVELY: RelayManager::shutdown is one client.disconnect() over the whole pool, reached from every burst teardown here (_shutdownPublishPool) and at step 9b of every Android delivery cycle plus onDestroy — so on BOTH background planes a relay carrying exactly one circle in a pass sees connect-at-its-own-publish through disconnect-at-teardown, a tail that grows with the circles published after it and converges over the CSPRNG permutation to the whole pass length. Only in the FOREGROUND is there no collective disconnect: publish_relay_options() is ping(false).reconnect(false).sleep_when_idle(true).idle_timeout(10 s) polled once a minute, so each relay's socket sleeps independently in (60 s, 70 s] after that relay's own last send. Presence is revealed to a circle relay at every burst instant. Since PUB-COALESCE one burst publishes EVERY publish-eligible circle, so for an eligible circle the REQ/CLOSE pair and this device's kind-445 for that circle now coincide on essentially every burst — the fractional mismatch this clause used to disclose is gone for that class. Four classes still produce a re-anchored #h REQ with no kind-445 for the circle it re-anchored: (a) the burst publishes NOTHING when openBurstPublishWindow returns null (no identity, disclosure not accepted, location permission revoked, one-shot GPS timeout) or consent flips inside the pass — the open precedes the publish unconditionally; (b) a circle in the stored live set that is not publish-eligible is re-anchored on every burst and never published to at all. The two sides are read from different places, and the subscription side is a STORED SNAPSHOT: resume_burst re-anchors active.group_subs, which only subscribe_circle, unsubscribe_circle and the relay-update paths mutate, all of them driven by LiveSyncResubscriber._applyDelta off a circlesProvider emission — and nothing re-derives it while backgrounded (the coordinator drives its work by direct call precisely because a provider invalidation schedules a rebuild a paused app never performs). So the subscribed set is every ACCEPTED circle AS OF THE LAST FOREGROUND EMISSION (groupsForCircles), while the publish target is re-read FRESH at encrypt time (encrypt_location -> get_circle -> circle.relays) and filterPublishEligibleCircles additionally excludes isLegacyOrphaned and engine-flagged Unrecoverable circles, so this is a permanent mismatch rather than a fractional one; (c) a per-circle send that fails or is DEFERRED by the MLS engine, and the tail of a roster past kMaxCirclesPerBurst (11), which the burst itself defers to the next tick; (d) a circle-set or relay-set change applied DURING the background window, where the two sides diverge because only one is re-read — a circle REMOVED while backgrounded keeps its #h REQ re-anchored on every burst with no kind-445 behind it, unbounded until the next foreground emission reaches _applyDelta, and a RELAY-SET change applied while backgrounded leaves the OLD relays subscribed and the NEW ones published to, so each set sees one half of the pair. Coalescing also LENGTHENS the exposure it narrows: the burst holds its connection across the whole staggered publish pass, so the connect-to-disconnect span grows with the number of eligible circles — saturating at the cap — and is a single-relay estimator of that count for every relay in the union resume_burst connects, inbox relays included (PUB-COALESCE). An inbox-only relay sees the same pair on every INBOX_BURSTS_PER_REQ-th burst with no kind-445 to pair it with, which is itself the inference that this pubkey is background-sharing now. The three RELAY-CONTACTING Dart maintenance timers — KeyPackage, relay-list, and the 15-minute subscription-health tick — are foreground-only on this branch (suspendForBackground cancels all three at the pause; health is gated again where it fires, the other two at arming only), because the burst IS the repair, at 72-168 s rather than 15 min. The FOURTH timer is not: the ~45 min public-profile anti-entropy sweep keeps its armed timer, gates at FIRE time (_appIsForegrounded) and RE-ARMS itself on the backgrounded branch, so it is a periodic CPU-only wake between bursts that contacts no relay. The complementary arm: every OTHER pause STOPS the engine rather than pausing it (MapShell.shouldStopLiveSyncOnPause = !(isIOS && backgroundSharingEnabled)), including iOS with background sharing off, and the Android foreground service shuts its own publish pool at the end of every cycle.
invariants.residual: 'enforced' is the BEHAVIOUR; parts of the pause ORDER, most of the Dart teardown, and one whole exception rest on less. (1) The five-step pause order is only PARTLY pinned. The Rule-13 link — the in-flight publish gauge before the radio cut — is pinned twice: rule13_a_burst_never_pauses_with_a_pending_publish_outstanding asserts the source order in BOTH pause_subscriptions and resume_burst's failure exit (and that neither cuts through a bare client.disconnect()), and pause_never_disconnects_while_an_auto_commit_awaits_its_ok proves it over a relay withholding a real OK. The drain-before-clear link has two oracles (pause_subscriptions_drains_the_intake_before_it_clears_the_router, a_pause_marker_drains_every_queued_event_before_the_router_is_cleared). Pinned by NOTHING: the placement of the unsubscribe sweep relative to the Pause marker, and of repair.clear() at the end — only their end states are asserted. check_engine_client_options.sh check 8 pins PRESENCE and deliberately not order (docs/POWER_EFFICIENCY_PLAN.md §5.4 says so in as many words); it is additionally fail-open on a terminate_all_relays() call wrapped in `if false`, on RELAY_TERMINATE_ROUNDS = 0, on an aliased shutdown(), and on a bare client.subscribe(...) in the burst-open path, and it opens neither config.rs, cursor.rs nor any Dart file. (3) The cold-launch exception has NO test anywhere in the repository: the race is MapShell's un-awaited _startLiveSync against _onPaused, MapShell is never mounted host-side (it needs the Rust bridge — every map_shell_*_test.dart is a predicate, collaborator or source-scan test), and the only host-visible seam, LiveSyncResubscriber, knows nothing of the app lifecycle. invariants.title: One standing connection lets a relay link identity to circle membership
invariants.statement: While the app is FOREGROUNDED, a single persistent socket per relay carries both the inbox filter naming the user's own pubkey (gift-wrap #p) and every subscribed circle's routing-tag filter (#h), so a relay serving both planes can correlate identity to circle membership by connection continuity — the ephemeral per-message 445 author keys do not prevent this, and on a new install the inbox and per-circle relay sets seed from the same defaults so the overlap is the default configuration. For CIRCLE relays the standing form is now foreground-only: backgrounded on iOS with sharing on the two filters ride ONE BOUNDED BURST PER PUBLISH TICK and the join is per-burst rather than continuous, and every other pause stops the engine outright. Per-burst is not per-publish, but since PUB-COALESCE it is much closer to it: a burst re-anchors EVERY circle's #h REQ, connects the whole relay union, AND publishes every publish-eligible circle, so for an eligible circle the join now coincides with that circle's own kind-445 on essentially every burst. It stays strictly wider in three cases — a burst whose publish window refuses publishes nothing at all; a subscribed circle that is not publish-eligible (isLegacyOrphaned, or engine-flagged Unrecoverable) is re-anchored on every burst and never publishes; a deferred or failed send, and the tail of a roster past kMaxCirclesPerBurst, re-anchors without a kind-445 — and the join is no longer instantaneous: the connection is held across the coalesced publish pass, whose length grows with the number of eligible circles and is therefore itself a single-relay estimator of that count. That is a narrowing, NOT a strict one: an inbox-ONLY relay — one holding the user's kind-10050 inbox but none of their circles, an independent set — carries no kind-445 to correlate with, and where it used to see one continuous socket it now sees a REQ/CLOSE pair every 72-168 s (the 120 s nominal cadence, jittered ±40 %), which is itself the inference that this pubkey is background-sharing right now. Raising INBOX_BURSTS_PER_REQ removes that cadence at the cost of background invitation latency (OD4-b, accepted, not yet raised); at the shipped value the inference is disclosed rather than mitigated. Both planes still open from the same address in the same seconds, so the two-socket join by source address is unchanged.

event_kinds.note: The inbox-plane filter side of the correlation: a #p filter naming the reader's own pubkey. Standing while foregrounded; backgrounded on iOS it rides every INBOX_BURSTS_PER_REQ-th publish burst, which is the residual cadence an inbox-only relay reads.

The group-plane filter side: an #h filter naming each subscribed circle's routing tag. Standing while on screen; on iOS-bg one bounded burst per publish tick — every burst re-anchors every circle AND publishes every publish-eligible one, so the join coincides with this circle's own kind-445 on essentially every burst, and the burst's connection is held across the whole staggered pass.

invariants.title: Timing and size metadata stay visible; jitter narrows it but padding does not exist
invariants.statement: The publish cadence is jittered uniformly over [nominal*(1-0.4), nominal*(1+0.4)] = [72 s, 168 s] from a CSPRNG, which defeats short-window rhythm fingerprinting but not long-run averaging; message sizes are NOT padded, so location updates fall in a narrow, recognisable size band. Narrowing the Rust spread without the Dart endpoints, or presenting the jitter as defeating traffic analysis, falsifies this.

tests.name: the production stagger draws from a CSPRNG

invariants.title: One burst publishes every eligible circle; only the CSPRNG stagger keeps their created_at stamps apart, and how much it buys shrinks with the roster
invariants.statement: Circles publish in ONE jittered burst per interval — up to kMaxCirclesPerBurst (11) of them, the rest deferred to the next tick, a branch kMaxCirclesPerAccount (10) keeps out of production reach — with consecutive encrypts at least kPublishStaggerMinGap (2 s) apart, so no two circles share a kind-445 created_at. The per-gap CEILING is kPublishStaggerMaxGap (9 s) only for small bursts: PublishStagger.maxGapFor prices each gap at the burst's own size, so it shrinks to 3333 ms at kMaxCirclesPerAccount (10) — the largest burst a bounded roster produces — and to a flat 3 s one circle further on, at the cap. The per-circle schedules this invariant used to enforce are gone, and so is the claim they carried: every relay carrying ANY of your circles now sees the same burst rhythm, so relays each holding only ONE of your circles can match the timing and tell those circles belong to the same phone. Two costs the record did not previously carry, both stated here rather than in the deviation alone. FIRST, the surviving archive claim is NARROWER than 'the stagger is the archive-adversary defence': after coalescing the archive reader gets the link anyway, from the shared inter-burst interval sequence. What the stagger still buys is ROSTER-SCOPED, because the observer reads no milliseconds — only floor(created_at) — so its alphabet is the whole-second delta, and maxGapFor thins that alphabet monotonically as the burst grows: {2..9} (eight values) at n <= 4, {2..6} at n = 6, {2..5} at n = 8, and {2,3,4} at n = kMaxCirclesPerAccount (10), the largest burst a bounded roster produces; {2,3} is maxGapFor's answer one circle further on and no observer reaches it while the bound holds. Both production call sites price the gap at the real burst size — the foreground tick through sampleGaps(count), the background pass through sampleGap(totalPublishes: total) where total is _encrypted.length + pending.length. COALESCING CAUSED THE THINNING: pre-P5 every gap was priced at the default totalPublishes = 2, so the alphabet was always eight. At small rosters the downgrade in KIND is real — a byte-identical created_at is a zero-cost equality join over a whole-network index (created_at_A == created_at_B, decisive on a single burst), while eight admissible offsets force a windowed correlation that must first hypothesise WHICH two circles share a device and then test that against a sequence of offsets. AT THE ROSTER BOUND IT BARELY IS: a three-element alphabet is three shifted equality joins over that same whole-network index, still un-targeted mass linkage, so what survives at ten circles is a constant factor rather than a change in kind. SECOND, coalescing makes the NUMBER of circles you are in a SINGLE-RELAY observable. Backgrounded on iOS the burst's engine socket connects the WHOLE relay union — every circle's relays AND the inbox relays (relay_union) — at the open and disconnects at the pause after the staggered pass, so the connect-to-disconnect span grows by one stagger gap per additional eligible circle (mean 5.5 s while the per-gap ceiling is the full 9 s, narrowing toward 2.5 s as the burst approaches the cap, the pass bounded by kPublishStaggerMaxSpread = 30 s) and is measurable server-side by ANY relay in that union: one carrying a single circle of yours, or an inbox relay carrying none of them. Sharply: the old scheme leaked the circle count only as a RATE, to shared relays that already read it off the multiplexed #h filter; the new one leaks it as a DURATION, to relays that previously could not know it at all. The account bound caps that estimator at ten, one circle under where the per-gap ceiling saturates. Restoring per-circle schedules is not the fix and is not proposed (it never decorrelated anything at a shared relay, and cost one radio wake per circle per interval); what falsifies THIS entry is a burst that publishes two circles inside one whole second, a stagger drawn from anything but a CSPRNG, or a per-gap floor at or below one second.

invariants.title: The eight profile relays and the six discovery relays never overlap, and neither carries circle traffic
invariants.statement: profile_relay_pool_default() has exactly eight entries, PRODUCTION_DISCOVERY_RELAYS exactly six, the two sets are disjoint by construction, and the profile pool is disjoint from the account seed defaults that carry kind-445/1059 traffic; this becomes false if a URL is added to one pool that already appears in the other, or if a pool relay is seeded into the circle plane.

invariants.title: No published event names the profile relays
invariants.statement: RelayType::Profile::to_kind() returns None, so no NIP-65 kind-10002 (or any other event) is ever built that serializes the profile relay list; this becomes false the moment Profile maps to a publishable kind or the list is written into an event's tags.

invariants.title: Profile lookups ask one relay about one person, bounded at two relays
invariants.statement: Every kind-0 filter carries exactly one author, no p tag and kind 0 only; each author resolves to its own assigned relay by salted rendezvous hash, and PROFILE_MAX_RELAY_RANK = 2 caps the retry ladder — so a lookup discloses an author to at most two of the eight. This becomes false if authors are batched into one filter, if the rank cap is raised, or if a fetch fans out beyond the assignment.

invariants.title: The assignment salt is zeroized, redacted and destroyed with the identity
invariants.statement: The per-install salt is ZeroizeOnDrop, renders redacted in Debug, never crosses the FFI, and is destroyed by BOTH the profile-delete path (wipe_all_profiles drops the row) and the logout wipe (the user_settings row is its only persistence, so deleting the circles.db file set takes it with it); this becomes false if a second identity on the same device can inherit the first's salt.

invariants.title: Two contacts can be assigned the same profile relay (P1)
invariants.statement: Assignment hashes the pubkey against a per-install salt with no knowledge of roster membership, so for a small circle several members genuinely can land on one pool relay; the spreading property is statistical, not an invariant.

invariants.title: Publishing your own profile reaches every usable pool relay (P2)
invariants.statement: publish_metadata targets the entire usable profile pool (it fails closed on an empty relay set rather than narrowing), so every pool relay learns (our pubkey, our IP) on every save; a subset publish would make the user invisible to peers assigned elsewhere.

event_kinds.note: Published to the whole usable pool via publish_metadata.

invariants.title: The eight profile relays are contacted unconditionally and see the device's IP (P3)
invariants.statement: usable_profile_relays() unions the eight defaults back in on every resolution, so the pool is contacted even when every user-chosen relay is private and a removal in Settings does not take effect; what the missing kind-10002 buys is only that relays OUTSIDE the pool get no public pointer to it.

invariants.title: The profile-relay pairing is durable by design (P5)
invariants.statement: The per-install salt is minted once and never rotated on a schedule, because each rotation would disclose every contact to an additional relay; the accepted cost is that the assigned relay accumulates a durable record that this IP keeps asking about this pubkey. The pairing still shifts for roughly 1/N of authors whenever the resolved pool changes.

invariants.title: Every host Haven contacts sees the real IP (P6)
invariants.statement: There is no Tor, proxy or onion transport: pool relays, circle relays, the tile provider and any host serving a co-member's profile picture observe the device's IP, and the co-member picture fetch happens automatically with no user action.

invariants.title: Relay exposure already incurred cannot be undone (P7)
invariants.statement: The contamination ledger is append-only, and Welcome-delivery relays from before the change were never persisted so refresh_contamination_ledger cannot fold them in; the UI can therefore only warn about an overlap it knows of, and excluding relays can shrink the profile pool below its usable floor.

invariants.title: MLS, circle and sync state are SQLCipher-encrypted on disk
invariants.statement: The sync-state and relay-state tables are unreadable in the raw database file without the keyring-held key, and an account wipe leaves nothing decryptable behind; this becomes false if a table is written outside the encrypted database or the wipe stops deleting the file set.

invariants.title: The map-tile cache is encrypted, capped at seven days, and wiped on identity deletion
invariants.statement: Tile blobs are stored only as SQLCipher-encrypted rows keyed by (style,z,x,y,retina) with the Stadia api_key stripped in Dart before the FFI, kTileMaxRetention is seven days and is the value the privacy copy quotes, and the wipe runs inside NostrIdentityService.deleteIdentity; this becomes false if a raw URL or api_key reaches the store, if the retention constant and the copy diverge, or if the wipe leaves the delete path.

invariants.title: The member directory records people, never which circle they came from
invariants.statement: member_directory carries exactly six columns — pubkey, is_current, last_shared_day, tier, rank_key, purge_after — and is WITHOUT ROWID, so it stores no implicit arrival-order counter either; no statement naming that table may also name a circle, group or MLS identifier; sync_co_members writes the UNION across all circles in one pass, so no row is attributable to a circle even by write timing. This becomes false if the table gains such a column by DDL or by a migration ALTER, if it regains a rowid (each pass inserts its NEW pubkeys in sorted order, so a descending pubkey step between consecutive rowids marks a batch boundary — a circle's roster), if a companion table re-creates the person-to-circle join beside it, or if a second writer outside the directory storage module inserts one.
invariants.residual: NO CIRCLE IDENTIFIER IS STORED; a limited circle inference is still available to an adversary holding the decrypted database. Everyone who leaves in the same day bucket freezes on the same last_shared_day, so a departure COHORT is visible, and for a user with few circles that cohort often IS one circle's roster. Day bucketing raises the cost of that re-partition and does not eliminate it (docs/MEMBER_PICKER_PLAN.md §6.1, which drops first_seen_day AND updated_day — the two columns that carried departure timing — along with second-granularity stamps and, since the WITHOUT ROWID conversion, the implicit rowid, precisely because each of them made it cheap). The bucket does not cross the FFI either: DirectoryEntryFfi carries pubkey_hex, npub and tier and nothing else, so the cohort stamp is legible only to someone reading the decrypted table directly, never to the UI layer. Scope: for CURRENT circles the same adversary can already read the full partition out of the engine's session.sqlite, so the directory only adds partition information for circles whose other rows delete_circle has already cascaded away.

invariants.title: A departed co-member is deleted from the directory three days later
invariants.statement: DIRECTORY_RETENTION_DAYS is 3 (259 200 s, owner decision D3, reduced from a drafted 7); a co-member absent from the union freezes at purge_after = (last_shared_day + 3) * 86400 and is removed by prune_expired_directory_members DELETING the row, never by a read hiding it, and a deliberate removal in either direction deletes the row immediately. The deadline binds the DISK, not only the display: the purge runs at every process start (CircleManager::new, a bare DELETE needing no MLS session and no roster read), inside the ranked read's own transaction before it selects, and in every reconcile — so the three days hold on an install that never opens the picker and never reconciles. Every one of those sweeps is the same comparison against the DEVICE WALL CLOCK — chrono::Utc::now() at process start, DateTime.now() marshalled as now_unix_secs for the ranked read and the reconcile — with no monotonic floor anywhere in the path, so the deadline binds only while that clock does. This becomes false if the constant changes, if an expired row is filtered out of a read instead of deleted, or if any of those three sweeps stops running.
invariants.residual: TWO RESIDUALS, BOTH IRREDUCIBLE AT THIS LAYER AND BOTH NOW OWNER-ACCEPTED RATHER THAN OPEN (decision D9, 2026-08-28, docs/MEMBER_PICKER_PLAN.md §10). (1) THE DEADLINE IS ENFORCED BY THREE ON-DEMAND SWEEPS, NOT BY A TIMER. An expired row is deleted at the next process start, at the next ranked read, or at the next reconcile — whichever comes first — and no read can return one, because the read sweeps inside its own transaction before it selects. What remains is the interval between the deadline and the next of those events on a device where the app never runs at all: the row is still on disk, unread by anything, until the process that would read it starts and erases it first. THAT ENFORCEMENT MODEL IS A DECISION, NOT AN INTERIM STATE: a timer and a background wake were both considered and declined under D9, because they buy the earlier deletion of a row nothing can read — the ranked read sweeps inside its own transaction before it selects — at the price of periodic wakeups. (2) THE CLOCK IS UNTRUSTED IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, and there is no monotonic floor anywhere in the path. A forward jump purges EARLY, which costs recent contacts and is self-healing for current members. A BACKWARD jump is the mirror case and is worse for the promise: purge_expired is DELETE ... WHERE purge_after < ?1, so a rolled-back clock makes every one of the three sweeps a no-op — expiry is not delayed but suspended — and because the ranked read's in-transaction sweep is that same comparison, a row past its window stays both STORED and RETURNABLE for as long as the clock reads earlier than its deadline. Closing this needs a trusted clock: SQLCipher offers no monotonic counter and a boot-relative clock does not survive a reboot, so it is stated rather than fixed, and D9 accepts it in the same breath as the sweep model; the eventual copy may not resolve it by promising a fixed wall-clock window. It is stated because a disclosure claiming a fixed window depends on it — and that copy (owner decision D6) has had no surface since the Settings → Privacy page was removed on 2026-08-29, which is why this entry carries no disclosure key. There is no wording for a copy-tie test to pin to DIRECTORY_RETENTION_DAYS; the constant itself stays test-enforced (retention_is_the_owner_decided_three_days). The drafted paragraph and its clause-by-clause constraints are preserved in docs/MEMBER_PICKER_PLAN.md D6.

invariants.title: The member directory exists only inside the encrypted circles.db
invariants.statement: The directory is stored only as rows in the SQLCipher-encrypted circles.db whose key lives in the platform keyring, and in no SharedPreferences/NSUserDefaults entry, flutter_secure_storage item or sidecar file — so deleting the circles.db file set is the whole of the logout guarantee, and that deletion is DEVICE-LOCAL rather than absolute: on iOS the file set sits in the backed-up Documents directory and a same-device restore can reinstate a pre-logout snapshot (accepted deviation IOS-BACKUP, owner decision D8). This becomes false if any Rust, Dart or native path gives those rows a second home the logout deletion does not reach. The Dart half of the guard scans the directory surface discovered BOTH by filename convention and by import closure over the row/staged-pick/query-fold modules — a convention-only scan left member_avatar.dart, search_fold.dart, create_circle_page.dart and add_member_page.dart outside it, so a preferences write from any of them would have passed.
invariants.note: Status stays 'enforced' under owner decision D8 (2026-08-28), which accepts the iOS backup posture unchanged. What this invariant checks is that the rows have NO SECOND HOME — no preferences entry, no secure-storage item, no sidecar file, no second Connection — and an iOS backup is not a second home Haven writes: it is the OS copying the one home wholesale, still inside SQLCipher, still keyed by a ThisDeviceOnly Keychain item. The rows are never outside the encrypted container, which is the claim as titled, so a downgrade would report Haven's storage discipline as partly enforced when it is not partly anything, and would spend the ratchet's signal on the event this row exists to catch: the day a real second home appears. What the backup DOES falsify is the corollary — 'deleting the file set destroys it' read as absolute — and that corollary is now scoped in the statement and registered as deviation IOS-BACKUP, whose forbidden_claim binds the copy. Status 'accepted_deviation' was not available: rule 9 requires a disclosure, and the member-directory disclosure (decision D6) has had no surface since the Settings → Privacy page was removed on 2026-08-29; a zero-disclosure accepted deviation is permitted since that date, so filing one is a deliberate act, not done here.

invariants.title: FLAG_SECURE covers every Activity in the Android process
invariants.statement: HavenApplication.onCreate registers an activity-lifecycle callback that SETS FLAG_SECURE in onActivityCreated, no Activity sets it per-Activity, and the manifest still names HavenApplication — so the block covers the photo-crop Activity and any future plugin Activity, not just MainActivity. This becomes false if any one of those four links is removed.

invariants.title: On iOS only the app-switcher snapshot is blurred
invariants.statement: iOS offers no FLAG_SECURE equivalent, so nothing prevents an in-app screenshot or screen recording by a circle member; the only protection is the app-switcher blur, installed on applicationWillResignActive (not didEnterBackground), covering the window itself, removed and re-armed only on applicationDidBecomeActive, with no UIApplicationSceneManifest that would stop UIKit calling those callbacks. This becomes false if any one of those links is removed.

invariants.title: The camera is used only by the QR scanner
invariants.statement: The only camera consumer is qr_scanner_page.dart via mobile_scanner in barcode-detection mode; no still capture, no video recording, no write to disk and no upload path exists. This becomes false if any capture or file-write API is added on that page.
invariants.residual: Nothing fails if a capture-to-disk or upload call is added to the QR page: the only citable proof is that the usage description still exists in Info.plist. The content claim 'No photos or video are taken or stored' has no test and no guard.

invariants.title: A photo picked from the library becomes a public profile picture
invariants.statement: The only consumer of a library-picked image is the profile avatar pipeline, which uploads it to the public Blossom host and references it from a public kind-0 — there is no private or circles-only destination, and the iOS permission prompt says so at the moment consent is given.

invariants.title: Identity creation collects no personal identifier
invariants.statement: Identity creation takes no email, phone number or password: the Identity model carries only pubkeyHex, npub and createdAt, and the secret bytes are never a field on it. This becomes false the moment a PII field is added to identity creation or to the identity model.
invariants.residual: No guard forbids adding an email/phone parameter to createIdentity or a PII field to Identity; the cited tests pin the model's current shape and the secret's absence from it, not the absence of a future field. The 'no sign-up' half rests on review.

invariants.title: Location is encrypted on the device, readable only by the circle
invariants.statement: A location update is MLS-encrypted client-side before any network write and decrypts only under the originating circle's epoch keys; a member of another circle holding the same ciphertext cannot read it. This becomes false if any plaintext coordinate is written to a relay or if cross-group decryption starts succeeding.

invariants.title: Haven runs no server of its own for circle traffic
invariants.statement: Publishes target exactly the user's own relay list and the live-sync engine connects only to configured relays, never a gossip-discovered one — there is no Haven-operated endpoint in the location path. This becomes false if any publisher or engine client acquires a hardcoded first-party destination.
invariants.residual: The 'you choose which ones to use' half is NOT true of the whole app: the eight profile relays and six discovery relays are contacted unconditionally and cannot be removed (INV-P-P3), the Blossom host is hardcoded to blossom.primal.net, and the tile provider is hardcoded to Stadia. Nothing fails if that gap widens. See the report's copy-defect section — onboardingValueProp2Summary's 'a relay network you choose' is contradicted by the code (usable_profile_relays() re-unions the curated pool); the Privacy-page paragraph that said so in the user's own words was removed on 2026-08-29, so nothing in the app corrects the onboarding claim any more.

invariants.title: A relay can only be added over wss://

invariants.title: The one-time kind-10051 retraction is disclosed while it is pending
invariants.statement: After the Dark Matter cutover Haven emits an empty replaceable kind-10051 to retract the retired KeyPackage relay-list advertisement, and the Relay settings page says so until the tick completes; this becomes false if the note is shown when nothing is pending, or hidden while it is.
invariants.residual: The two relay_settings_page_test.dart cases that exercise the note are named with concatenated Dart string literals, so no single-literal test name exists to cite under the checker's declaration rule; and no test pins that the retraction actually completes. The disclosure's timing rests on those uncitable widget tests.

invariants.title: Roster and circle name rest on one confidentiality layer, not two
invariants.statement: Group-control kind-445s (commits and proposals) are MLS PublicMessage under the engine's PURE_PLAINTEXT_WIRE_FORMAT_POLICY — signed and integrity-protected but NOT MLS-encrypted — so the roster, member credentials (each member's Nostr identity pubkey), their 0xF2F1 identity proofs and the circle name carried inside them are protected by the outer exporter-keyed ChaCha20-Poly1305 wrap ALONE. Application messages are double-sealed: OpenMLS encrypts them unconditionally regardless of the wire-format policy, so a location sits inside an MLS PrivateMessage inside that same outer wrap.
invariants.residual: Nothing in this tree fails if an MDK bump changes the wire-format policy or the exporter derivation; the only levers are pinned_dependencies.mdk_rev and the grep-based check_no_exporter_label_override.sh. Upstream itself marks the policy WIRE_FORMAT_POLICY_REVIEW_REQUIRED ('Revisit Before External Rollout'). So the confidentiality of the circle's NAME and MEMBER LIST is single-layered while the location half is not — a future change could silently downgrade one and not the other.

event_kinds.note: Commits/proposals ride the same kind as application messages but a different MLS wire format.
